title: 2036: A Very Canadian Space Defence Operation
summary: It’s 2036, and Canada has spent fifteen years building a sovereign space-defence architecture. Then, a foreign satellite moves, GPS starts failing in the Arctic, and someone probes a ground station in Ontario. Canadian Armed Forces personnel start putting the pieces together using the new systems, but an operational gap left behind by the buildout slows them down.
articleHtml:
It is the year 2036

Canada has been building and modernizing its defence space architecture for 15 years. The following systems are online and functional, providing the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) and Department of National Defence (DND) with unprecedented sovereign aerospace capabilities:

Systems that watch the Earth:

  • Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radar (A-OTHR): Operational since 2029 and built by the Australians, this ground-based radar reflects signals off the upper atmosphere, allowing Canada to detect aerospace threats thousands of kilometres away, over the curve of the Earth.
  • Defence Enhanced Surveillance from Space Project (DESSP): Coming online a year ago, this constellation of radar satellites allows the military to see through clouds and in complete darkness.
  • Polar Epsilon 2 (PE2): Satellites that, amongst other things, compare radar images against the positions that ships broadcast.
  • Canada Lynx (fictional): Twelve small satellites in three orbital planes for radio frequency transmissions and positioning. This is a follow-on from the Gray Jay Pathfinder mission from the mid-2020s.

System that watches Earth’s orbits:

  • Surveillance of Space 2 (SofS2): Canadian satellites that track objects in space, providing Space Domain Awareness (SDA).

Communications:

  • Enhanced Satellite Communications Project — Polar (ESCP-P): Military satellites that provide satellite communications (SATCOM) capability in the Arctic.

Systems that aggregate, fuse, and interpret the data:

  • Modernized Command and Control Information System (MC2IS): A suite of integrated systems that provide pan-domain command and control capability to the military in real-time.
  • Information Technology Infrastructure in Support of Command and Control (ITI in Sp of C2): It replaced the previous generation of separate classified networks for the military with one secure network.
  • Space Command and Control Information System (SC2IS). A modern command and control system for Canada, bought from the United States, that ingests and fuses space data to provide a real-time operating picture of outer space. It also integrates with MC2IS.
  • Cloud-Based Command and Control (CBC2): The Air Force’s cloud computing and AI-supported system to process monitor and control Canadian airspace.
  • Pan-Domain Command and Control (PDC2): The military’s doctrine to run operations across all operational domains. Every staff course in the country teaches it now.

Systems that put systems into space:

  • Canso, Nova Scotia: An operational rocket launch site that can be used to put satellites into orbit, with multiple commercial rocket providers.

In this setting, our story takes place…

Day 1

7 Space Operations Squadron (7SOPS) HQ, Ottawa, 03:47 hrs

Corporal Richard Straw, working the overnight shift at the 7SOPS watch-floor, glances up at the large central screen that covers most of the front-wall. His eyes are drawn to a yellow box on the live SC2IS dashboard reading 31% anomaly score. As trained, he pulls it up on his personal terminal to dive deeper.

The system has linked three events from the previous two weeks into a correlated anomaly:

  1. A foreign commercial satellite manoeuvring off its nominal path.
  2. A couple of intermittent and erratic GPS degradations across Canada’s western Arctic.
  3. An unconfirmed attempt to probe the scheduling system at Durham Earth Station, a commercial satellite ground station in Bruce County, Ontario.

He pushes the alert to Major Nadine Sauve, Space Warfare Officer and the Officer in Charge of the watch-floor. His job is done.

Maj. Sauve’s job is to track unusual space events and make the call every young-officer working nights dreads — whether to wake-up the CO or not. She reads the correlation report twice, and then files it for next Tuesday’s Commander’s Brief. 31% is not significant enough for a 4AM wake-up call.

7 Space Operations Squadron Detachment, North Bay, 06:10 hrs

Sergeant Ray Kirkland opens the same alert at the start of his shift at the 7 SOPS secondary facility, embedded within 22 Wing for continuity of operations, and not yet at full operational status. He works down the hall from the Canadian Air Defence Sector, where the CBC2 analysts monitor Canadian airspace for NORAD. At breakfast the previous morning he had overheard one of them complaining about a run of GPS reports from northern route crews, all of them out west, and none of them adding up to anything.

The alert on his screen reminds him of the conversation. The pattern concerns him — it is too regular for a natural cause and too scattered for an equipment fault — and now the system has flagged it as correlated.

He calls Maj. Sauve in Ottawa to talk it through.

Canadian Embassy, Berlin, 14:20 hrs

Over coffee, a German official asks Ambassador Paul Levesque if Canada had noticed anything “unusual” with any of their satellites. In the universal language of diplomacy, this means: I have intelligence I cannot legally share, but you should probably look into this.

Paul, who had absolutely no idea what she was talking about, responded with the universal diplomatic translation for I am completely clueless:

“We’re assessing the situation.”

Day 2–3

Ottawa and North Bay

Maj. Sauve and Sgt. Kirkland examine the problem together over the secure link established as part of the IT Infrastructure upgrades, using various analysis tools embedded within SC2IS and MC2IS. These systems are designed precisely for this type of analysis.

Together with GPS degradation reports from Transport Canada, characterized satellite telemetry from SofS2, and cyber-security traces from Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, part of the Communications Security Establishment (CSE), they begin putting together a combined picture.

The AI system also flags fishing vessels off Labrador for unusual identification activities, reported by the Marine Security Operations Centre (MSOC). They spend seven hours checking it out, only to discover that these were genuine fishing boats with faulty AIS transmitters.

Seven hours wasted because the AI got a bit over-zealous. They return to focusing on the three correlated events.

Ottawa, 11:30 hrs

Maj. Sauve was one of the first direct intake cohorts of the Royal Canadian Air Force’s Space Warfare Officer occupation — making her one of the few people in the military who had spent their entire career working in the space domain. During her trade qualifications, she remembered, they covered “Pan-domain Command and Control” in some detail, especially as it related to space. One concept that stuck with her through the years was:

An adversary who intends to hide their actions will first attack your ability to detect them.

So she asks a different question: What detection tool could a potential adversary want to degrade?

She asks SC2IS to extrapolate the anomalous satellite’s trajectory until its covariance matrix overlaps a Canadian asset, in plain French. After thinking for 34 seconds, the system spits out an answer: the anomalous satellite’s covariance ellipse will overlap with CanadaLynx-2 RF satellite within the next 24 hours.

Ottawa, 11:48 hrs

The anomalous satellite’s operator files a routine notice of space operations, announcing a radar test.

Maj. Sauve receives the notice via her terminal. They’re telling us what they’re about to do.

No need to wake up the CO now — he is already on the watch-floor with her, following the situation live.

Durham Earth Station, Bruce County, 20:00 hrs

Captain Marcus Oyelaran, a full-time Reservist within 32 Signal Regiment, arrives at the Ground Station antenna site that sends command and control signals to ESCP-P. He is accompanied by a section of Combat Engineers (Sappers) from 32 Combat Engineer Regiment who will set up perimeter security and a checkpoint on the only road leading into the site.

Ruth, the site manager, has worked the station for nineteen years and has never needed soldiers before. Concerned, she asks Capt. Oyelaran, “Are we expecting something?”

“I think we just don’t want to be surprised”, responds the Captain, who is quite unsure of exactly why he is here himself. His Warning Order informed him that there was suspicious network activity happening at the site, and that his Signals training, along with his twelve years of experience working as a civilian IT engineer, made him the right candidate to lead this temporary assignment. He was to report to the site and wait for further instructions.

“Yes, Sir”.

Soon after arrival, Capt. Oyelaran examines the property: One high-speed fibre route to a standard corporate network scheduling system, with digital access through credentials and physical access through cards. Everything seemed standard.

Early next morning he is asked to escort a Network Engineer from the site’s commercial operator to a junction box, where she replaces a card. Nobody tells him why, and he knows better than to ask.

Day 4

Arctic, 06:02 hrs

CanadaLynx-2's primary transceiver stops responding. A few minutes later, its emergency transmitter stops transmitting. The satellite is now a broken washing-machine in space.

The anomalous satellite’s operator files a report: it has concluded a routine radar test.

Technically true. What they did not mention was that the test had directed a short, extremely high-power RF transmission into CanadaLynx-2’s receive chain. The primary receiver failed first. The satellite switched automatically to its backup, which failed a few minutes later.

Ottawa, 07:00 hrs

Maj. Sauve briefs the Commander of 3 Canadian Space Division, Brigadier General Omer Ali Hamza, her boss’s boss’s boss, at an emergency Commander’s Brief at the National Defence Headquarters. She states that the act was deliberate and targeted. She also claims that the adversary likely attacked this satellite over others because it is capable of detecting GPS jammers in Canada’s West.

“Can we still find the jammers without it?”, asks the BGen.

“We can get a circle, but not a dot,” she responds. In the Arctic, a circle is a pretty big place — a fact that does not need to be stated, everyone in the room knows.

“How quickly can we replace the downed satellite?”

“Ten or eleven days, if we can launch a spare from Canso,” responds Maj. Sauve’s boss, Lieutenant Colonel Jennifer Leblanc, the Commander of 7 SOPS. “It used to take fourteen months. Thank God for tactical launch!”

“Let’s start the Operational Planning. Back-brief to me at 10:00 hrs. I’ll let the boss know,” concluded BGen Hamza, swiftly heading off to his meeting with the Chief of Defence Staff.

Canso, Nova Scotia, 13:40 hrs

Anjali Menon receives a call that a spare DND satellite is on its way to Canso from Markham, Ontario, for a rapid tactical launch. As a former SpaceX engineer and current Chief Engineer at Canada’s first sovereign orbital launch pad, she has overseen several launches. This one, however, is tricky — not because of the rocket — she has a choice of those — but because of the orbit. The replacement satellite must reach almost the same orbital slot as the dead satellite within eleven days.

The Earth rotates Canso, situated on Canada’s Atlantic coast, through the path twice a day. This gives her two narrow launch windows, if the weather and logistics cooperate.

She begins the paperwork.

Day 5

Durham Earth Station, Bruce County, 12:40 hrs

At the check-point, Master Corporal Jonathan Lee, a part-time Reservist and proud Sapper, is having lunch with Capt. Oyelaran. MCpl Lee volunteered for this short posting, thankful that his civilian employer, a software engineering company located in downtown Toronto, allowed him the time off on short notice.

Having finished his “boxed-lunch”, a typical meal given to CAF members working away from a dining hall, he leans back and tells Capt. Oyelaran about the time an employee at his job resigned while on maternity leave. Since the resignation was unusual, he said, the IT department forgot to revoke all her access. Her personal phone remained connected to the company’s internal messenger, and the issue was only discovered when she messaged “Why am I still receiving these messages?” in a group-chat a few months later.

Capt. Oyelaran stops talking. He had now been briefed about why he was there — because some unknown actors had somehow gained access to the satellite scheduling system, but it was proving difficult to find out who and why.

MCpl Lee’s words get him thinking. He immediately visits Ruth’s office and has a long discussion about what else may have access to the scheduling systems. Not who, but what — are there other machines, or software, that have credentials to access the system?

Ruth says she doesn’t know, but will pass on the question via email. MCpl Lee would never learn that his off-handed anecdote told over a cold tuna sandwich is the reason Canada’s only sovereign SATCOM system never gets successfully polled again by unauthorized parties.

Day 6

Durham Earth Station, Bruce County, 02:30 hrs

Somebody attempts a login to the scheduler again using a third-party contractor password. This time, however, the attempt fails because the credentials were revoked three hours earlier. The location of the hacker is traced by CSE, past four layers of proxies, to the operator of the anomalous satellite.

A few days later, on their way back to Toronto for redeployment, Capt. Oyelaran tells the Sappers, “A couple of days ago somebody tried the front door of the software again and this time it was locked. Our job is done.”

When asked who it was, Capt. Oyelaran honestly responds that he does not know.

Days 7

The GPS jamming in the Arctic is still a circle, and nobody has figured out why it’s happening. All parties continue to keep detailed logs of on-going events.

Day 8

“Still assessing the situation?” asks the German liaison.

Paul Levesque, now armed with more information but no resolution, responds with the standard answer:

“Still assessing the situation.”

Day 11 — Launch

Canso, 07:14 hrs

The Canadian rocket launches four minutes into the launch window while Anjali watches it from inside the control room. She has done this a few times, but it’s always nerve-racking.

The room is quiet through ignition, and remains quiet through stage separation. A few minutes later, the payload, CanadaLynx-13, separates, to a smattering of applause. Watching over the virtual feed, BGen Omer Ali Hamza thanks the team for their efforts — launching a replacement satellite in eleven days is a tremendous feat for a country like Canada that, only ten years earlier, had no sovereign launch capability.

Day 13

Ottawa and North Bay, 15:22 hrs

Over the next day and a half, CanadaLynx-13 uses a series of small burns to settle into position. Once there, the constellation re-gains the four-spacecraft geometry needed to locate the interference with useful accuracy.

The circle becomes a dot on the MC2IS live dashboard.

Then, it becomes five dots.

This was not one jammer. This was a line of buoys in the icy waters off Canada’s North-West coast.

Backtracking through the timelines, the full picture was now formed using the MC2IS historical data logging system:

A commercially registered ship had deployed the buoys late in the previous summer in one voyage. Canada’s Arctic Over-the-Horizon Radar had tracked the ship throughout its voyage, one of several thousand surface contacts the system logs every week. Nothing about its track was unusual.

The ship stopped transmitting its position for one day during a real solar disturbance, and filed a fault-report shortly thereafter. Polar Epsilon 2 had flagged the transponder gap and matched it against a DESSP radar pass from the same night. The radar showed the ship roughly forty kilometres from its last reported position. A vessel drifting off its reported track during a solar disturbance is unremarkable, so the MSOC analysts logged the events and closed the case, which would have been the correct thing to do.

The buoys remained dormant for months until activated by the adversary. Each buoy transmits short bursts on its own schedule, causing periodic and asynchronous GPS jamming that is difficult to track.

Ultimately, a combined team of Joint Task Force (North) and Canadian Rangers pulls one buoy out of the ice and ships it to Defence Research and Development Canada (DRDC) for reverse engineering.

Day 14

Berlin, 11:00 hrs

Paul Levesque finally has the full picture thanks to an intelligence brief.

An adversarial state gained access to one of Canada’s satellite scheduling systems by opportunistically phishing a third-party contractor who had built a dashboard for its commercial operator. This led to them monitoring Canada’s satellite command and control for several months. Simultaneously, they realized that maneuvering one of their older radar satellites would put it in the direct path of CanadaLynx-2, which was one of the key assets monitoring Canada’s Western Arctic. Combining the two attack vectors, they initiated a disruption and degradation campaign in key shipping lanes. The goal, it seems, was not to attack Canada in any significant way, but to mask their activities in the waters and keep Canada guessing indefinitely.

They likely had not expected Canada to be able to put the pieces together in a few days, or launch a replacement satellite in eleven. There had been no disruptions recorded since the discovery of the jammers, and the anomalous satellite had maneuvered back into its old slot.

Of course, Paul did not have clearance to share any of this with his German counterpart. So when he was asked next time, he responded with,

“There was a minor nuisance with one of the satellites. We have dealt with the situation, and the matter is now closed.”

The German liaison knew exactly what that meant.

Day 19

Ottawa

Maj. Sauve runs the original analysis again, but this time assuming the GPS data from Transport Canada and digital traces from CSE were available on Day 1, when CanadaLynx-2 was still online.

Anomaly score: 81% — She would have definitely woken the CO for this.

In other words:

Nothing had failed. The systems, software, and personnel all acted as they should have. Everything Canada had spent years building came together beautifully.

However, every organisation that held a piece of the puzzle held it in isolation. Transport Canada, CSE, MSOC, and 7 SOPS each did exactly what they were mandated to do, but no system in Canada was permitted to integrate the data and share it with the right parties autonomously, at the right clearance levels. Information was still shared by humans, in the form of reports, who worked 9–5 during weekdays.

Integrated, the data would have produced an anomaly score of 81% on Day 1, which could have saved a Canadian satellite, fourteen days of uncertainty, and tens of millions of dollars.

Either way: Canada learned a lesson, and the adversary learned about Canada’s readiness and capabilities.

Day X

7 Space Operations Squadron HQ, Ottawa, 22:32 hrs

Capt. Jerome Brown, Space Warfare Officer, receives a note from an operator on the watch-floor.

Four correlated events, anomaly score of 29%.

He calls the CO.
